newsitem.title: YEMEN: Candidates make final pitches in Yemen election.
newsitem.headline: Candidates make final pitches in Yemen election.

text.p: Candidates toured Yemeni villages on Saturday to make their final pitches before a parliamentary election on Sunday which officials hope will bring stability and ease economic hardships caused by the 1994 civil war.
A total of 2,306 candidates including 17 women are seeking 301 parliamentary seats under the banner of 12 parties or as independents.
Western diplomats expect President Ali Abdullah Saleh's ruling General People's Congress (GPC) to win the majority of seats, followed by its coalition partner -- the Islamist Islah Party.

The main opposition Yemen Socialist Party (YSP), some of whose former leaders launched the southern separatist campaign that sparked the war, and three others have announced they will boycott the poll to protest against alleged irregularities.
Saleh has denied the opposition charges.
The government is banking on the election to project abroad an image of democracy that will build investor confidence needed to speed recovery and improve the limping economy.

Western diplomats say if Saleh's GPC returns as the governing party, it could manage the delicate task of pressing ahead with economic reforms agreed with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
The reforms are a sensitive issue in a land where marginal increases in the price of bread or petrol can unleash unrest.
Yemen, a small independent oil producer, is one of the Arab world's poorest countries and some Yemenis are worried that reforms could bring more austerity.

In the city of Dhalaa in Lahj governorate, 320 km (200 miles) south of the capital Sanaa, thousands of opposition party members demonstrated on Saturday and called on voters to boycott the elections, residents said.
They said the protest was peaceful as security forces kept a close watch.
The country is still paying a heavy political price from the war, in which a secessionist bid by the south was crushed by northern forces loyal to Saleh.

Western diplomats and officials say democracy is the only way to keep together a country with a history of revolutions, border clashes, civil wars, political assassinations, riots and often bloody feuds.
But the diplomats say Yemen's road to democracy involves a delicate balance between reforming the political system and taking into account traditional factors such as powerful tribes.

Candidates range from a popular singer to the president's son to parliamentary speaker Sheikh Abdullah Bin Hussein al-Ahmar, known for his skill in mediating between the government and volatile tribes in times of crisis.
In recent years, tribes with grievances against the government have kidnapped scores of foreign tourists and diplomats to use as bargaining chips.
